Language: Python; license: MIT; created 2026-09-03; last push 2026-11-18
Latest release: v3.13.2 (2026-11-18)
README (start):
Give your coding agent a video editor.
Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP client edits your footage with local FFmpeg, then checks its own output.
No cloud · No API keys · Python standard library

```bash
npx ffmpeg-skill
```

  
    caption.py --animate pop --karaoke
    fit.py --aspect 9:16 --fit crop
  
  
    silence.py --threshold -35
    loudness.py -I -14 --tp -1
  

Left half is the input, right half is what the command produced. **[Every before/after demo, with the exact command under each one →](docs/demos.md)** — all of it built by `python3 demos/build.py`, so you can rebuild every frame of it yourself. The footage is synthetic (FFmpeg's own test sources) except in three demos, `reframe_talk`, `filler_en` and `pauses_en`, which use two AI-generated clips of people who do not exist ([demos/footage/](demos/footage/README.md)).

`ffmpeg-skill` is an [Agent Skill](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/agent-skills) for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and any agent that reads `SKILL.md`. It teaches the agent a fixed workflow (probe → edit losslessly where possible → check → verify) and ships **42 tools** that do the actual work with `ffmpeg` / `ffprobe`: cut, join, silence removal, fit to duration and aspect, captions and karaoke, overlays and motion graphics, HDR → SDR and LUTs, audio clean-up and typed dynamics, sync with drift correction, multicam, loudness, delivery checks, whole-edit project rendering, batch folders. Every tool is also callable as an MCP tool (`tools/list` advertises a core 12 by default to keep client context small, with `FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_FULL=1` listing all 42; every tool is reachable by name through `tools/call` either way), and the whole set is described by a machine-readable contract.

If `ffmpeg` and `python3` are on your PATH, it works: offline, on footage you would rather not upload.

- **Protect your source files.** A destination that matches a declared input is refused. Direct edits require `--overwrite` to replace an existing output. A `batch --watch` job can replace an unchanged file it delivered on an earlier pass. The `-y` in the dry-run command takes effect only after the tool checks the destination.
- **Call typed tools.** The agent supplies named options such as `--aspect 9:16` and `--fit pad`. The tool builds the FFmpeg command and filter graph.
- **Verify the edit.** The tools probe the source and the written file, so the agent can check the actual duration, frame size and audio before reporting success.

> **SPEC** (Self-Producing Execution Contract): each tool's `input_schema` — the part of its
> contract and MCP tool definition that has to track the CLI flag-for-flag — is never
> hand-authored beside the code. It is derived, at run time, from the same `argparse` parser that
> already defines the CLI, and CI fails the build if any of it drifts.
> → [full explanation](#what-is-spec)

---

## Standalone, and in an ecosystem

**Standalone**, this is a local FFmpeg engine: probe → edit → verify, `npx ffmpeg-skill` and nothing else. No API key, no account, no other repo required. Everything above and below this section describes that standalone tool, and none of it changes if you never read the rest of this one.

**In [kajisho5](https://github.com/kajisho5)'s wider video-production ecosystem**, this repo is the *hands*: it cuts, measures and exports files, and reports back in structured JSON. It does not decide what to cut, whether a deliverable is approvable, what makes a highlight interesting, or what a caption should say (the user's cue text is burned as written, never rewritten to fit) — those are a *brain*'s job, sitting in front of this engine, not inside it.

| You want to... | Use |
|---|---|
| Cut / join / measure / export a file right now | **this repo** (`ffmpeg-skill`), standalone |
| Decide cut points, approve a deliverable, plan a whole edit | [`video-production-agent`](https://github.com/kajisho5/video-production-agent) / [`AI-video-production-OS`](https://github.com/kajisho5/AI-video-production-OS) |
| Build a typed editing graph across a workspace, without writing raw `ffmpeg` | [`video-editing-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/video-editing-skill) / [`audio-production-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/audio-production-skill) |
| Put Remotion motion graphics (animated captions, silence jump cuts, audio-peak motion) on a real recording | [`remotion-ffmpeg-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/remotion-ffmpeg-skill): its compositions take their length, fps, frame, silences, scene cuts, audio peaks and beats from this repo's `probe.py`, `silence.py` and `scenes.py`. It verifies its render with `check.py` and `look.py`, composites a graphics layer with `overlay.py` (`--place` for its `--sparse` mode), and delivers through `render.py --template` |

Other repos in the ecosystem — [`media-analysis-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/media-analysis-skill), [`transcription-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/transcription-skill), [`subtitle-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/subtitle-skill), [`thumbnail-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/thumbnail-skill), [`color-grading-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/color-grading-skill), [`motion-graphics-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/motion-graphics-skill), [`qc-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/qc-skill) — read this repo's `contract --json`, its tools' `--json` output and `doctor`, the same way any agent framework would; this repo does not call into any of them. The dependency runs one way.

## Why

An agent that "knows FFmpeg" still guesses: it assumes a frame rate, picks a codec the container cannot hold, re-encodes a file that only needed a stream copy, and reports "done" without opening the result. This skill takes the guessing out:

- **Real files first.** Every job starts with `probe.py`; the agent decides from the measured duration, fps, resolution, colour and audio layout, not from the file name.
- **Structured tools, not shell strings.** Each operation is a script with typed arguments. Nothing runs through a shell; no filter graph is accepted from the caller.
- **A contract the agent can read.** `contract --json` states, for every tool, what it takes, what it writes, which FFmpeg components it needs and how the result is verified. The MCP surface is derived from it.
- **Verification after execution.** The result is probed, checked against the destination's spec and, when the picture changed, looked at as a contact sheet.
- **Local first.** No cloud, no API keys, no Python dependencies. Optional local transcription is used when a speech engine (Parakeet or a whisper) is installed, never required — by `caption.py --transcribe` and, since 1.17, by `silence.py --transcribe` (with `--filler`, or since 3.6 with `--sentence-min-silence` / `--sentence-margin-tail`); both take a transcript you already have instead, and both refuse with the install lines rather than guessing. Both take `--engine` and `--model`; `FFMPEG_SKILL_ASR_ENGINE` and `FFMPEG_SKILL_ASR_MODEL` set this machine's defaults (e.g. `large-v3-turbo` where that whisper.cpp model is installed; without either, auto and `base`). The engine runs on your machine and the audio is never uploaded; parakeet-mlx, faster-whisper and openai-whisper download their model weights the first time they run (parakeet-mlx's default from Hugging Face).

## Paper

The design discipline behind this skill — per-operation verification for AI agents — is written up as a position paper. The paper scores ffmpeg-skill itself as only partially conformant with the discipline it defines.

Kajiyama, S. (2026). *What Is Verification-Driven Coding? — A Discipline for Not Trusting Generation.* Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23720216

## Quick start

```bash
# 0. FFmpeg itself, once (Ubuntu/Debian shown; macOS and Windows are in the Install table below)
sudo apt install ffmpeg

# 1. install the skill for Claude Code (Cursor: --cursor, Codex: --codex, all three: --all)
npx ffmpeg-skill

# 2. check the machine: ffmpeg, ffprobe and every FFmpeg component the tools need
npx ffmpeg-skill doctor

# 3. (for agent frameworks) read the machine-readable contract
npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json | head -40
```

Captions from speech (`caption.py --transcribe`) need one local speech engine, installed separately. `pip install faster-whisper` is the simplest; the first run downloads its model, and the audio never leaves the machine. Without an engine, everything else works, `doctor` lists the engine as missing optional, and `--transcribe` refuses with the install line for each engine it supports.

Already installed? re-run `npx ffmpeg-skill` to refresh `~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill`. Copies are not updated automatically.

`doctor`'s overall `ok` and a single tool's `usable` are different signals: `ok` is false when anything *some* tool requires is missing, so one missing filter (a plain Homebrew `ffmpeg` without `subtitles`, or a build without libvidstab) turns it false even though most tools still run. Check `doctor --json`'s `tools` field for the per-tool answer, not just `ok`.

Then talk to your agent:

> "Take `interview.mp4`, keep 0:45–1:20 and 5:00–5:25, and make it a 60-second Reel."

The agent runs `probe.py`, `cut.py --segments 0:45-1:20,5:00-5:25 --accurate`, `fit.py --aspect 9:16 --fit crop`, `export.py --preset reels`, `check.py --platform reels` and `look.py`, then reports "final.mp4: 60.00 s, 1080×1920, 30 fps, AAC stereo" with the contact sheet it inspected.

### Deliver to a platform

One command per destination, with the app's own UI taken into account:

```bash
python3 $S/render.py talk.mp4 --template tiktok --cues cues.txt
```

That fills the shipped `templates/tiktok.json`: 9:16 crop, captions popped word by word *above*
TikTok's description bar and clear of its like column, −14 LUFS, the `tiktok` export preset, and
a `check.py --platform tiktok` on the file it wrote. The caption size comes from the delivery
table, so since 1.17.1 the filled project also states `"fit_size": "on"`: a size nobody asked for
shrinks to fit the cue instead of splitting the sentence across two cues. A template that states
its own `fit_size`, and a `--brand` that states a caption size, still win, and a project with
`"fit_size": "off"` renders the captions 1.17.0 rendered. Templates ship for `tiktok`, `reels`,
`shorts`, `youtube-shorts`, `youtube`, `x`, `linkedin`, `facebook`, `podcast` and `audiogram`;
`--template all` (or a comma-separated list) renders the seven video destinations (`tiktok`, `reels`, `shorts`, `youtube`, `x`, `linkedin`, `facebook`) from the same edit and
writes a `_pack.md` table of what each one produced. Files land next to the input unless
`-o` says otherwise, and `--dry-run` shows every planned command rather than a result.
`render.py --list-templates` prints them with their frames, limits and safe zones. Alias
spellings work everywhere a platform is named (`youtube-shorts` = `shorts`, `ig` = `reels`,
`twitter` = `x`, `fb` = `facebook`).

The tools also work on their own, from any shell:

```bash
S=~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill/scripts
python3 $S/probe.py input.mp4 --compact
python3 $S/fit.py input.mp4 --duration 60 --method trim --aspect 9:16 --dry-run    # plan a trim and reframe
python3 $S/export.py input.mp4 --preset reels --json                 # structured result with a probe of the output
```

## How to build with Docker

Begin by cloning the repository and building the Docker container:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk
cd rustdesk
git submodule update --init --recursive
docker build -t "rustdesk-builder" .
```

Then, each time you need to build the application, run the following command:

```sh
docker run --rm -it -v $PWD:/home/user/rustdesk -v rustdesk-git-cache:/home/user/.cargo/git -v rustdesk-registry-cache:/home/user/.cargo/registry -e PUID="$(id -u)" -e PGID="$(id -g)" rustdesk-builder
```

Note that the first build may take longer before dependencies are cached, subsequent builds will be faster. Additionally, if you need to specify different arguments to the build command, you may do so at the end of the command in the `` position. For instance, if you wanted to build an optimized release version, you would run the command above followed by `--release`. The resulting executable will be available in the target folder on your system, and can be run with:

```sh
target/debug/rustdesk
```

Or, if you're running a release executable:

```sh
target/release/rustdesk
```

MoviePy (online documentation [here](https://zulko.github.io/moviepy/)) is a Python library for video editing: cuts, concatenations, title insertions, video compositing (a.k.a. non-linear editing), video processing, and creation of custom effects.

MoviePy can read and write all the most common audio and video formats, including GIF, and runs on Windows/Mac/Linux, with Python 3.9+.

# Example

In this example we open a video file, select the subclip between 10 and
20 seconds, add a title at the center of the screen, and write the
result to a new file:

``` python
from moviepy import VideoFileClip, TextClip, CompositeVideoClip

# Load file example.mp4 and keep only the subclip from 00:00:10 to 00:00:20
# Reduce the audio volume to 80% of its original volume

clip = (
    VideoFileClip("long_examples/example2.mp4")
    .subclipped(10, 20)
    .with_volume_scaled(0.8)
)

# Generate a text clip. You can customize the font, color, etc.
txt_clip = TextClip(
    font="Arial.ttf",
    text="Hello there!",
    font_size=70,
    color='white'
).with_duration(10).with_position('center')

# Overlay the text clip on the first video clip
final_video = CompositeVideoClip([clip, txt_clip])
final_video.write_videofile("result.mp4")
```

# How MoviePy works

Under the hood, MoviePy imports media (video frames, images, sounds) and converts them into Python objects (numpy arrays) so that every pixel becomes accessible, and video or audio effects can be defined in just a few lines of code (see the [built-in effects](https://zulko.github.io/moviepy/reference/reference/moviepy.video.fx.html) for examples).

The library also provides ways to mix clips together (concatenations, playing clips side by side or on top of each other with transparency, etc.). The final clip is then encoded back into mp4/webm/gif/etc.

This makes MoviePy very flexible and approachable, albeit slower than using ffmpeg directly due to heavier data import/export operations.

ffmpeg-skill measures the footage. Remotion draws from those measurements. ffmpeg-skill checks and delivers the result.

An Agent Skill for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex that puts Remotion motion graphics on real recordings — and never guesses a number. Composition length, fps and frame size come from the probe; cuts come from measured silences; pulses hit on measured audio peaks; captions keep the timing of your SRT. Every render is verified frame-for-frame against its timeline and inspected with a contact sheet before it ships.

Built on ffmpeg-skill. Unofficial — not affiliated with Remotion.

Fictional demo footage. ffmpeg-skill measured two silences and a scene cut; Remotion played only the speech ranges with punch-in zooms and re-timed captions; render.py verified 201 of 201 frames.

Karaoke — words light up at their measured times (250 / 250 frames verified)	
9:16 + Japanese — silences cut, CJK font staged automatically, phrase-based line breaks
Why this and not just Remotion's own skills?

Remotion's official Agent Skills teach an agent to write good Remotion code. This skill closes the loop around it:

	Remotion skills	remotion-ffmpeg-skill
Writes Remotion compositions	✅	✅ (three ready-made, timeline-driven)
Knows the source's real duration / fps / size / silences / scene cuts / audio peaks	—	✅ measured by ffmpeg-skill
Never draws on VFR or HDR footage as is: refuses it, or (--conform) draws on a CFR, SDR BT.709 copy ffmpeg-skill made, original untouched	—	✅
Verifies the render (exact frame count, fps, size, audio)	—	✅ non-zero exit on mismatch
Looks at the result (contact sheet)	—	✅
Delivers for YouTube / Reels / TikTok / Shorts / X with loudness and compliance checks	—	✅ ffmpeg-skill templates + check.py

They work well together: install both if you write custom compositions.

Install
npx ffmpeg-skill              # the measuring/delivery half (required)
npx remotion-ffmpeg-skill     # this skill, next to it in ~/.claude/skills

--cursor, --codex, --all, --project work for both. Requirements: Python 3.10+, Node.js 18+, FFmpeg (ffmpeg-skill's doctor tells you what's missing). Remotion's headless browser downloads itself on the first render.

What you can ask for
"Put animated captions from talk.srt on talk.mp4 and make it a YouTube upload."
"Cut the silences out of this recording, jump-cut style, and keep the subtitles in sync."
"Make graphics that hit on the loud moments of clip.mp4, as a Reel."
"Here are my chapters (0:00 Intro …): put them on screen and make it a YouTube upload." — a card at each chapter start, chapter markers in the file, and the description block to paste.
"Caption talk.mp4 from the transcript transcription-skill made, words lighting up as they're spoken." — analyze.py --words talk.transcript.json; the transcript's schema version is checked and its times are used exactly as written.
"Japanese captions, vertical, for TikTok." — renders 9:16 with a blurred fill, stages a CJK font automatically, breaks lines between phrases.
Under the hood
S=~/.claude/skills/remotion-ffmpeg-skill/scripts

python3 $S/init.py ./motion --install                       # Remotion project (pinned versions)
python3 $S/analyze.py talk.mp4 --captions talk.srt          # -> talk.timeline.json (all measured)
python3 $S/still.py  --project ./motion --comp Jumpcut --timeline talk.timeline.json --at 2
python3 $S/render.py --project ./motion --comp Jumpcut --timeline talk.timeline.json -o jumpcut.mp4
python3 $S/deliver.py jumpcut.mp4 --platform youtube        # template + compliance table

# or all of it, each step verified before the next:
python3 $S/pipeline.py talk.mp4 --project ./motion --comp Jumpcut --captions talk.srt --platform youtube

Every script takes --json, --dry-run, --overwrite, --timeout, like ffmpeg-skill.

MCP
claude mcp add remotion-ffmpeg-skill -- python3 ~/.claude/skills/remotion-ffmpeg-skill/mcp/server.py

Tool names and input schemas come from the machine-readable contract (npx remotion-ffmpeg-skill contract --json), generated from the scripts' own argument parsers.

Compositions
Id	Length	What it draws
Captioned	source duration	caption cards that spring in on each cue (text exactly as written)
Jumpcut	sum of measured speech ranges	silences removed, punch-in on every other cut, captions re-timed
PeakPulse	source duration	edge glow + zoom on measured audio peaks or beats, flash on scene cuts, progress bar
Titled	source duration	your lower thirds, a title card at each measured scene change, a card at each chapter start
Highlights	sum of ranked highlights	ffmpeg-skill's audio-energy highlights back to back, counter, title
BeatMontage	source duration	audio unbroken, picture cuts on the measured beat grid
Karaoke	source duration	words light up at the times a local speech engine measured
Emphasis	source duration	YouTube-style captions: the words you name (or the captions' own numbers / names) pop, change colour or get a box when spoken; speech bubbles and comment cards
Pip	source duration	a second recording (camera) in a corner, synced by the offset measured between the two audio tracks; captions on top

Any shape: --aspect 9:16 | 1:1 | 4:5 | 16:9 with --fit blur | contain | cover; pipeline.py --platform reels picks 9:16 from ffmpeg-skill's own template so nothing gets cropped on delivery.

Fonts: Japanese / Chinese / Korean captions get the CJK font ffmpeg-skill finds on the machine, loaded before the first frame — no tofu. --font-file for your own.

A layer for your editor: --overlay --keep-graphics renders the graphics alone as transparent ProRes 4444 and composites it over the untouched source with ffmpeg-skill — keep the .mov for Premiere, Resolve or Final Cut.

One brand file for both skills: --brand brand.json reads ffmpeg-skill's own brand file — colours, caption colour, font, font file — and on delivery the template places its logo, so graphics drawn here match what ffmpeg-skill draws.

Colours, font, caption size, zoom and pulse strength are options (--options look.json); the timeline format and every option are in references/timeline.md. Add your own composition to the generated project and render it with --comp YourId.

What render.py verifies
jumpcut.mp4: 6.32 s, 1280x720, 30.0 fps, audio
  size      PASS  1280x720 (expected 1280x720)
  fps       PASS  30.0 (expected 30.0)
  frames    PASS  189 (expected 189)
  audio     PASS  present (expected present)
Look: jumpcut_sheet.png

Frame numbers are Math.round(seconds × fps) on both sides (TypeScript and Python), so the expected count is exact, not "close enough".

Licence

This skill is MIT. Remotion itself has its own licence: free for individuals and for-profit organisations with up to 3 employees; larger companies need a Remotion company licence. Using this skill does not change that.

Speed

Remotion renders in a headless browser. Measured on a 2-core Linux machine: a 30 s 1080p30 render takes about 80 s (≈ 2.6× the clip length) with render.py's default of all CPU cores — Remotion's own default (half the cores) took 170 s. More cores scale it further. Check with still.py and --fast before a full render of long footage.

--sparse (Captioned, Karaoke, Titled): only the frames that show a caption, lower third or scene title are drawn; ffmpeg-skill places each stretch back at its time over the untouched source. Same picture frame for frame (checked by an integration test). How much it saves depends on how much of the footage shows graphics — measured on the same 2-core Linux machine, 1280×720, 30 fps:

Footage	Frames drawn	Full layer	--sparse
60 s, captions on 7 s	211 / 1800 (12 %)	152 s	46 s
40 s, two scene titles + one lower third	272 / 1200 (23 %)	104 s	39 s
60 s, captions on half of it	909 / 1800 (50 %)	155 s	100 s
captions on all of it	—	—	nothing to skip: draws the full layer and says so

Browser start-up and the final composite cost the same either way, so the gain is smaller than the share of frames skipped. Needs an ffmpeg-skill whose overlay.py has --place; otherwise it draws the full layer and says why.

Agent evals

Plain requests ("captions for YouTube", a Japanese Reels jump cut, "cut to the beat", a lower third without a name, a plain trim that is not this skill's job, a square highlight reel), run by an agent that only has the skill files, graded on what it leaves behind — plus a transparent layer for an editor, joining clips with titles, and karaoke from word timings: 9 / 9 (run 1, run 2, how to run). A third run with a neutral prompt (both skills installed, no hint) went to ffmpeg-skill alone for three requests it can finish by itself — 6 / 9 by the original checks, 9 / 9 once that route is accepted (run 3).

0.5. CI renders every composition on Linux, macOS and Windows (Node 22, Remotion 4.0.538, ffmpeg-skill main).

AI Video Production Orchestrator. kajisho5/ffmpeg-skill を Media Processing Engine (Hands) として使い、本リポジトリは Production Brain (Orchestrator) を担当する。

Project IR: docs/project-ir.md、ADR: docs/decisions.md
Phase 1 の範囲（実装済み）

Request → Requirements → Intent → Analysis(probe / silence / loudness) → Inference → Decision → Plan → Project IR → Validation → Execute(cut / loudness / export via ffmpeg-skill) → QA(probe / loudness / check / look) → Report / Provenance。

未実装（設計のみ）: conference パイプライン本体、Web UI、job queue。

依頼文（brief）から requirement を作る（ADR-061、requirements_extraction）: video-agent plan talk.mp4 --brief "60 s vertical, captions, -14 LUFS" は brief を --set と同じ key（edit.fit=9:16 / subtitle=true / audio.loudness.target_lufs=-14 / audio.normalize=true）に読む。読み手は AI provider（Claude provider、またはチャットのモデルが --brief-requirements answer.json で答える host provider）、どちらも無ければ決定的な規則（英語と日本語:「縦型」「字幕」「-14LUFS」など。範囲は agent/brief.py と ADR-061）。許可される key は --set を検証するコードから導かれ、未知の key・不正な値は理由付きで拒否、key の無いもの（「60秒」のような長さ）は適用せず理由を表示する。明示の --set が常に勝つ。AI が読んだ key は AI_GENERATED として記録され、それに基づく変更は CONFIRM になる。解析せずに読みだけ見るなら video-agent brief "縦型で字幕つき、-14LUFS"。

AI（Claude）: pip install -e '.[ai]' の上で VIDEO_AGENT_AI_PROVIDER=anthropic（資格情報は ANTHROPIC_API_KEY か ant auth login。モデルは VIDEO_AGENT_AI_MODEL、既定 claude-opus-5-5）。AI は計測結果と依頼文から制作の推薦を出すだけで、引用の無い推薦は捨てられ、実行の可否は policy と検証が決める（ADR-018 / ADR-049）。未設定なら完全に決定的なパイプラインのまま動く。

チャットの Claude を脳にする（API キー不要、ADR-050）: Claude Code / Claude Desktop など、いま話しているチャットのモデルが推薦を出す。手順は2段で、plan --ai-brief が AI に渡す材料（計測結果・引用可能な id・許可された intent・依頼文・規則）を出し、チャットのモデルがそれを読んで JSON で答え、revise <project> --ai-recommendations answer.json --ai-model claude-code がその答えを ADR-049 と同じ検証に通して新版にする（受理・却下の内訳を表示）。

Claude Code: OS の installer が SKILL.md を ~/.claude/skills/video-agent にリンクするので、「この動画を YouTube 用にして」と頼めば上の2段を CLI で回す。MCP で使うなら claude mcp add video-agent -- video-agent-mcp --workspace ~/video-agent-work。

{"mcpServers": {"video-agent": {"command": "/abs/path/to/video-agent-mcp", "args": ["--workspace", "/abs/path/to/video-agent-work"],

Audio / Video → Transcript.
The speech-recognition layer of the video-production toolchain: local faster-whisper, offline mode, timestamped segments and words, deterministic cache, JSON contract for agents. Nothing is uploaded, no API key exists.

Quick start · CLI · Library / tool contract · Security and offline guarantees · Documentation

  

pip install "transcription-skill[faster-whisper] @ git+https://github.com/kajisho5/transcription-skill"
transcription transcribe lecture.mp4 --language ja

transcription-skill turns speech in an audio or video file into a validated Transcript: segments with timestamps, optional word timestamps, language, confidence and full provenance, plus SpeechEvent-compatible candidates for a production agent to reason about later. Recognition runs on this machine with faster-whisper; nothing is uploaded, no API key exists.

transcription-skill is not a video editing agent. It does not decide what to cut, which camera to show, where chapters go, who is speaking, or how captions should look. It turns speech into timestamped text and stops there.

Quick start

Requirements: Python 3.9+, FFmpeg (ffmpeg and ffprobe on PATH), and an ASR engine. The package core is standard library only; the current Reference Local Engine, faster-whisper, is an optional dependency that runs Whisper on this machine (CPU or GPU).

# install (or, from a checkout: pip install -e ".[faster-whisper]")
pip install "transcription-skill[faster-whisper] @ git+https://github.com/kajisho5/transcription-skill"

# check the machine: ffmpeg, engine, cached models, workspace, path policy
transcription doctor

# transcribe
transcription transcribe lecture.mp4                       # auto language, writes lecture.transcript.json
transcription transcribe lecture.mp4 --language ja         # Japanese, no detection
transcription transcribe lecture.mp4 --word-timestamps     # per-word timing; every word numbered (`index`)
transcription transcribe lecture.mp4 --language ja --word-timestamps --word-segmentation dictionary
                                                           # Japanese dictionary words + part of speech (pip install "transcription-skill[ja]")
transcription transcribe lecture.mp4 --offline             # hard no-network constraint
transcription transcribe dubbed.mkv --audio-stream 1       # multi-track input: decode the 2nd audio stream, not ffmpeg's default pick
transcription transcribe meeting.wav --vad-filter           # skip non-speech before decoding (long recordings with real silence)
transcription transcribe talk.mp4 --engine haas_ja --language ja --vocabulary terms.json --word-timestamps
                                                           # optional Japanese engine (Linux + NVIDIA GPU), jargon/names list
transcription transcribe talk.mp4 --language en --programme programme.txt --slides pages/deck.json --speaker "Amaka Okonkwo" --corrections fixes.json
                                                           # terms from the programme / slides / speakers to the engine's prompt; timed post-corrections (ADR-047)
transcription transcribe talk.mp4 --engine speechcpp --language ja --word-timestamps
                                                           # optional engine: speech.cpp's `speech` (Metal/Vulkan/CPU, no Python ML, no CUDA)
transcription transcribe talk.mp4 --engine speechcpp --model parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 --language de --word-timestamps
                                                           # English and 24 other European languages on speech.cpp, with word times
transcription transcribe talk_en.mp4 --model distil-large-v3.5 --language en
                                                           # English-only distilled Whisper (faster-whisper 1.2.0+); other languages refused
transcription transcribe talk.mp4 --engine qwen3_asr --language ja --word-timestamps
                                                           # optional: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B + forced-aligned word times (11 languages)

# hand off
transcription export lecture.transcript.json --format srt -o lecture.srt
transcription export lecture.transcript.json --format tsv -o lecture.tsv  # start\tend\ttext per segment
transcription export lecture.transcript.json --format txt -o lecture.txt  # plain reading text, no timestamps
transcription segments lecture.transcript.json --merge-gap 0.5 --json   # SpeechEvent candidates
transcription cache size                                  # entries + bytes used in the transcript cache
transcription cache list                                  # cache key, size, created_at per entry
transcription cache clear                                 # remove every cached transcript
transcription models pull base                             # pre-fetch a model before going --offline
transcription models list                                  # every model's availability
transcription models remove base                            # free disk by dropping a cached model

Recognition never uses the network. The base model (~145 MB) is fetched into the Hugging Face cache once, on first use, or you place it there yourself for an air-gapped machine and run with --offline. Japanese and English are first-class in the tests and evals; the engine supports 100 languages.

Example output (real run on the committed fixture, faster-whisper base):

ja_short.wav: 9.61s, language ja (requested), 1 segment(s), engine faster_whisper 1.2.1 model base
  00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:08.360  本日の公園を始めます 宜しくお願いします まず最初に会場の音教設備についてご説明します

The homophone errors (講演→公園, 音響→音教) are what a small Whisper model produces on synthetic speech. The skill records them as-is: an ASR result is evidence, not an edited script.

Why a transcription Skill

An agent that calls "whisper" directly gets a text dump with no identity, no provenance and no boundary. This skill exists to make recognition a reusable, verifiable data step:

A Transcript is a contract, not a print-out. Segments, words, language and provenance are validated before anything is returned; timestamps are checked against the media; a document that fails validation is never produced.
Engines are interchangeable, the contract is not. faster-whisper is the implemented Reference Local Engine; every engine is described by the same EngineSpec (where it runs, whether it needs the network, which models are on disk) and picked by constraints, never by the skill's own opinion.
Same input, same result, no second run. The cache key is the content fingerprint plus engine, model and parameters; a cached transcript is returned without starting an engine process.
Offline is a constraint, not a hope. --offline refuses remote engines and any model download before anything runs.
Built to be called from another program. transcription run - takes one JSON request on stdin and answers with exactly one JSON document; transcription contract --json (alias: skill --json) publishes the tool and engine contract; input paths can be confined to allowed roots.
Ecosystem: PROCESS · MEASURE · TRANSCRIBE · DECIDE

Each repository answers one question and stops there.

repository	verb	question it answers	output
ffmpeg-skill	PROCESS	how is the media transformed?	cuts, encodes, captions burnt in, delivery files
media-analysis-skill	MEASURE	what exists in the media?	Observations: duration, streams, silence, loudness
transcription-skill	TRANSCRIBE	what is being said, and when?	Transcript, SpeechEvent candidates
subtitle-skill	PRESENT	how is it shown on screen?	subtitle files (SRT / WebVTT) from a typed request; burn-in delegated to ffmpeg-skill
video-production-agent	DECIDE	what should be done with it?	inference, decisions, production plans

A Transcript is a recognition result. It is not an Event (the agent lifts it into its timeline), not a Decision (the agent makes those), and not a Subtitle (subtitle-skill renders those). The plain SRT/VTT this skill can write are inspection views of the data, not subtitle design.

Engine ecosystem

transcription-skill is a transcription capability, not a faster-whisper wrapper. Every engine is described by the same machine-readable contract (EngineSpec: id, version, execution_mode, requires_network, capabilities, languages, models and their availability), lives in a registry, and is chosen by constraints, never by the skill's own judgement.

engine	execution_mode	status
faster_whisper	local	implemented, verified on the fixtures (Reference Local Engine)
haas_ja	local	implemented, optional: Haas-ja-v1.0 via haas-asr; Japanese only; Linux + NVIDIA GPU + Python 3.11+; custom vocabulary; unit-tested against a fake haas_asr, not yet run on a GPU (ADR-033)
speechcpp	local	implemented, optional: speech.cpp's speech command (0.10.0+ on PATH) on Metal, Vulkan or the CPU; ReazonSpeech v2 / parakeet-tdt_ctc-0.6b-ja / Haas-ja-v1.0 (Japanese, word timestamps), parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 (25 European languages, word timestamps; ADR-040) and Qwen3-ASR (30 languages, words null); models fetched with speech pull, never by the skill; unit-tested against a fake speech, the real binary runs in the engines CI job (ADR-035)

qwen3_asr	local	implemented, optional: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B with Qwen3-ForcedAligner-0.6B word timestamps (both Apache-2.0, pinned revisions) via qwen-asr (Python 3.10+, the [qwen3-asr] extra), on a CUDA GPU or the CPU; 11 languages; never downloads while transcribing (models pull once); unit-tested against a fake qwen_asr, the real models in the manual qwen3_asr job, not yet run (ADR-041)

LOCAL vs REMOTE. A local engine runs recognition on this machine; its only possible network use is a one-time model download, reported per model as MODEL_DOWNLOAD_REQUIRED (or MODEL_MISSING when downloads are impossible). A remote engine sends audio to another host and therefore has requires_network: true. --offline is a hard constraint, not a preference: remote engines are refused (ENGINE_UNAVAILABLE, reason network_required), a model that is not already on disk is MODEL_UNAVAILABLE (availability: MODEL_MISSING), and the engine is told not to fetch anything.

transcription engines --engine faster_whisper  # plus per-model av

Why use Skills

Skills are reusable, filesystem-based resources that give Claude domain-specific expertise: workflows, context, and best practices that turn a general-purpose agent into a specialist. Unlike prompts (conversation-level instructions for one-off tasks), Skills load on demand, so you don’t have to repeat the same guidance across conversations.

How Skills work

Skills use Claude’s VM environment to provide capabilities beyond what’s possible with prompts alone. Claude operates in a virtual machine with filesystem access, allowing Skills to exist as directories containing instructions, executable code, and reference materials, organized like an onboarding guide you’d create for a new team member.

This filesystem-based architecture allows progressive disclosure: Claude loads information in stages as needed, rather than consuming context upfront.

Skills can contain three types of content, each loaded at a different time:

Level 1: Metadata (always loaded)

The Skill’s YAML frontmatter provides discovery information:

---
name: pdf-processing
description: Extract text and tables from PDF files, fill forms, merge documents. Use when working with PDF files or when the user mentions PDFs, forms, or document extraction.
---


Claude loads this metadata at startup and includes it in the system prompt. The description is what Claude matches your request against when determining whether to trigger the Skill, so it must say both what the Skill does and when to use it. This lightweight approach means you can install many Skills without context penalty: until a Skill is triggered, only its name and description occupy context.

Level 2: Instructions (loaded when triggered)

The main body of SKILL.md contains procedural knowledge: workflows, best practices, and guidance:

# PDF Processing

## Quick start

Use pdfplumber to extract text from PDFs:

```python
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    text = pdf.pages[0].extract_text()
```

For advanced form filling, see [FORMS.md](FORMS.md).


When you request something that matches a Skill’s description, Claude reads SKILL.md from the filesystem using bash. Only then does this content enter the context window.

Level 3: Resources and code (loaded as needed)

Skills can bundle additional materials:

pdf-processing/
SKILL.md (main instructions)
FORMS.md (form-filling guide)
REFERENCE.md (detailed API reference)
scripts/
fill_form.py (utility script)

Instructions: Additional Markdown files (FORMS.md, REFERENCE.md) containing specialized guidance and workflows

Code: Executable scripts (fill_form.py, validate.py) that Claude runs using bash, providing deterministic operations without loading their code into context

Resources: Reference materials such as database schemas, API documentation, templates, or examples

Claude accesses these files only when referenced. The filesystem model means each content type has different strengths: instructions for flexible guidance, code for reliability, resources for factual lookup.

Skills run in a code execution environment where Claude has filesystem access, bash commands, and code execution capabilities. Skills exist as directories on a virtual machine, and Claude interacts with them using the same bash commands you’d use to navigate files on your computer.

How Claude accesses Skill content:

When a Skill is triggered, Claude uses bash to read SKILL.md from the filesystem, bringing its instructions into the context window. If those instructions reference other files (such as FORMS.md or a database schema), Claude reads those files too using additional bash commands. When instructions mention executable scripts, Claude runs them through bash and receives only the output (the script code itself never enters context).

What this architecture makes possible:

On-demand file access: Claude reads only the files each task needs. A Skill can include dozens of reference files, but if your task only needs the sales schema, that’s the one file Claude loads. The rest stay on the filesystem and cost zero tokens.
Efficient script execution: When Claude runs validate_form.py, the script’s code never loads into the context window. Only its output (such as “Validation passed” or a specific error message) consumes tokens, which makes scripts far more efficient than having Claude generate equivalent code during the task.
No practical limit on bundled content: Files don’t consume context until accessed, so Skills can include comprehensive API documentation, large datasets, or extensive examples. There’s no context penalty for bundled content that isn’t used.
Example: Loading a PDF processing Skill

Here’s how Claude loads and uses the custom pdf-processing Skill from the earlier examples (not the pre-built pdf Skill):

Claude calls: bash: cat pdf-processing/SKILL.md → Instructions loaded into context.
Claude determines: Form filling is not needed, so Claude doesn’t read FORMS.md.

Skills are available across Claude’s agent products. For Claude Managed Agents, see its Skills page.

Claude API

The Claude API supports both pre-built Agent Skills and custom Skills. Both work identically: list each Skill’s type and skill_id in container.skills.

Prerequisites: Using Skills through the API requires the code execution tool, whose container Skills run in.

Use pre-built Agent Skills by referencing their skill_id (pptx, xlsx, docx, or pdf), or create and upload your own through the Skills API (/v1/skills endpoints). For how custom Skills are shared, see Sharing scope.

Skills on the API run in a sandboxed container with no network access and no runtime package installation. See Limitations and constraints for details.

To learn more, see Using Agent Skills with the API.

Claude Code

Claude Code supports custom Skills. The pre-built document Skills (PowerPoint, Excel, Word, PDF) are not available in Claude Code, though the open-source Claude API skill comes bundled with it. See the full list of built-in commands and Skills that ship with Claude Code.

Custom Skills: Create Skills as directories with SKILL.md files. Claude discovers and uses them automatically.

Custom Skills in Claude Code are filesystem-based and don’t require API uploads: place them in ~/.claude/skills/ (personal) or .claude/skills/ (project).

To learn more, see Use Skills in Claude Code.

claude.ai

Pre-built Agent Skills: These Skills are active when you create documents. Claude uses them with no setup required.
